opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea behind Prismatic Synthesis is that what matters isn't just how big or strong your teacher model is. It's how *diverse* the resulting training data is, and diverse in a way that actually matters for generalization.

The field has mostly measured data diversity with surface-level proxies: lexical overlap, n-gram statistics, or embedding similarity from some sentence encoder. Those don't tell you much about whether two examples will teach the model different things. Two math problems can look very different on the surface but exercise the same reasoning, or look nearly identical but require quite different solution strategies.

So we proposed measuring diversity in the space of *gradients*. We take a small, off-the-shelf proxy model and compute the gradient each training example would induce. If two examples push the model's parameters in similar directions, they're redundant from a learning perspective. If they push in different directions, they're contributing something distinct. We then compute an entropy-style diversity score over those gradient representations, which we call G-Vendi. What was striking is that this metric correlated really strongly with out-of-distribution generalization across many different datasets, much better than the conventional diversity measures.

Once you have a metric you trust, you can use it to *steer* synthesis. That's where the "prismatic" part comes in. We cluster the existing data in gradient space and identify regions that are underrepresented, the sparse clusters. Then we have the generator produce new problems and solutions targeted at those sparse regions, filter for quality, add them, re-cluster, and iterate. Rather than sampling more and more from the high-density regions the teacher naturally gravitates toward, you deliberately spread the data out, like light through a prism.

The punchline is that using a much smaller teacher, on the order of a 32B model rather than a several-hundred-billion-parameter reasoning model, we could create a math reasoning dataset that, when used to train a student, matched or outperformed students trained on data distilled from the much larger teacher, and the gains showed up especially on out-of-distribution benchmarks.

The broader lesson I take from this is that scale isn't the only lever. A bigger teacher gives you higher-quality individual samples, but it also tends to give you a lot of the same kind of sample over and over. If you're smart about *where* in the learning space your data lands, a smaller model can be surprisingly competitive. That's encouraging for academic labs and for anyone who doesn't have access to the largest frontier models, because it means thoughtful data design can substitute for a good chunk of raw compute.

r001.rationale: It says larger teachers tend to produce “a lot of the same kind of sample over and over,” communicating that capable teachers generate homogeneous data.

r002.rationale: It explains that a small proxy model computes per-example gradients and that gradient similarity or difference indicates whether examples are redundant or diverse.

r003.rationale: It identifies sparse gradient-space clusters to target with new generations, but does not say examples are removed from overrepresented clusters.

r004.rationale: It describes iterating after adding and reclustering data, but does not say retained diverse examples are used to prompt the teacher in the next round.

r005.rationale: It says the smaller teacher’s data matched or outperformed data from a much larger teacher, but omits the one-million-example comparison and the 671-billion-parameter teacher.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the starting point for Prismatic Synthesis is a somewhat uncomfortable observation: when you generate synthetic math data with a model, the problems and solutions tend to cluster. You ask for a thousand problems and you get a thousand variations on the same handful of underlying reasoning patterns. The surface forms differ, the numbers change, but the gradient a student model gets from them is largely redundant. And the usual response is to scale the teacher, because a bigger model has more to say. That works, but it's expensive, and we wanted to know whether the real variable was teacher size or data diversity.

The core idea is to measure diversity not in the text but in gradient space. We take the student model, run the candidate examples through it, and look at the gradients each example induces. Then we cluster those gradients. Two problems that look very different on the surface but push the parameters in the same direction land in the same cluster. Two problems that look superficially similar but exercise genuinely different reasoning land in different clusters. That gives us a diversity metric we call G-Vendi, which is essentially the effective number of distinct gradient directions in a dataset, and it turns out to correlate much better with downstream performance than token-level or embedding-level diversity measures do.

Once you have that measure, the generation strategy follows naturally. Instead of just sampling from the teacher and keeping everything, we sample, map each new example into the gradient-cluster space, and preferentially generate more where the coverage is thin. We seed the teacher with examples from underrepresented clusters and ask it to produce problems in that neighborhood. So the small teacher is being steered, example by example, to fill in regions of reasoning space that the student hasn't seen much of, rather than being asked to be creative on its own, which small models are generally bad at.

The result that surprised us is how much this closes the gap. A roughly 7 or 8 billion parameter teacher, used this way, produced data that trained students to match or beat students trained on data from models an order of magnitude larger, when we held the number of examples fixed. And the effect is not just on in-distribution math benchmarks. The diversity gains transfer to out-of-distribution reasoning tasks, which is the part I find most interesting, because it suggests that what the big teacher was really contributing was coverage, not some ineffable quality of individual solutions.

I should be honest about the limits. The gradient clustering depends on the student you're training, so the data is tailored to that model family and may be somewhat less portable. And there's a cost to computing gradients for a large candidate pool, though it's small compared to the cost of serving a frontier model for synthesis. But the broader lesson I take from it is that we've been using teacher scale as a proxy for diversity, and diversity is the thing we actually want. If you can measure it directly and optimize for it directly, you can get a lot more out of smaller, cheaper, more open models than people have assumed.

r001.rationale: The response says generated problems and solutions cluster into repetitive reasoning patterns, even when they come from a larger teacher.

r002.rationale: It explains measuring diversity from gradients induced by examples in the student model, but does not identify that model as a small proxy model.

r003.rationale: It describes generating more examples for underrepresented clusters, but does not explain aggressively removing examples from overrepresented clusters.

r004.rationale: It says examples from underrepresented clusters are used to seed and prompt the teacher to produce more problems in those areas.

r005.rationale: It reports results for a 7–8-billion-parameter teacher against models an order of magnitude larger, but not one million examples or the specified 32-billion- and 671-billion-parameter teachers.

astra-6.text:
The key idea is that the teacher’s size isn’t the only thing that determines how useful its synthetic data will be. How you elicit that data—and the diversity and quality of the resulting examples—also matters.

Think of the prism metaphor: you take a math problem and explore different facets of it. You can change the assumptions, vary the difficulty, or ask for a different reasoning approach. Instead of repeatedly sampling very similar problems from the smaller teacher, you use it to produce a broader range of learning experiences.

But diversity alone isn’t enough, especially for math. You also need to check correctness and filter out examples where the solution doesn’t support the answer. Then you train the student on that curated collection.

So the goal isn’t to make the smaller teacher suddenly as capable as the larger one. It’s to extract more useful training signal from what it can already do. A diverse, carefully checked dataset from a smaller teacher can compete with a less thoughtfully constructed dataset from a much larger teacher.

r001.rationale: It says repeated sampling from the smaller teacher can produce similar problems, but does not state that even highly capable teacher models generate homogeneous synthetic data.

r002.rationale: It discusses varying problems and checking quality, but does not describe representing problem–solution pairs with gradients from a small proxy model to assess diversity.

r003.rationale: It mentions producing a broader range of examples, but does not explain removing examples from overrepresented clusters in gradient space.

r004.rationale: It says to train the student on a curated collection, but does not say retained diverse examples are used to prompt the teacher in a subsequent generation round.

r005.rationale: It makes a general comparison between carefully constructed and less thoughtful datasets, but gives no result comparing one million examples from 32B and 671B teachers.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea is to get more out of the smaller teacher by asking it to approach the math through different lenses. Instead of repeatedly prompting it to generate a problem and an answer, you vary the kinds of problems, the reasoning strategies, and the ways a solution is presented. Those different perspectives are the intuition behind “prismatic.”

But diversity alone isn’t enough, because you can also generate diverse mistakes. You need to check correctness and filter the examples, while preserving useful variation in difficulty and reasoning. Then you train the student on that curated mixture.

So the comparison isn’t simply a smaller teacher versus a larger teacher. It’s the quality and coverage of the resulting training data. A smaller model can be quite useful within its capabilities, and a carefully constructed dataset can make it competitive with data generated by a much larger model.

r003.rationale: It mentions filtering examples for correctness, but not removing examples from overrepresented clusters in gradient representation space.

r004.rationale: It says to train the student on a curated mixture, but does not say retained examples prompt the teacher in a subsequent generation round.

r005.rationale: It gives no one-million-example result or comparison between 32-billion- and 671-billion-parameter teachers.
